title: Module 0 · Hospital Pharmacy 101
intro: Start here if you have never worked in a hospital. How the queue, the chart, the MAR, the cabinets and the people fit together, and how to think through any order.

cases.title: Your first order in the queue
cases.setting: First shift · central pharmacy · verification queue
cases.stem: You log in and the first order is: **enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily** for a 78 year old woman admitted with pneumonia. It looks routine. Before you click verify, you need a system you run on every order, every time.

steps.q: What do you look at before you even read the drug?

options.t: Patient first: age, weight, allergies with reactions, pregnancy
options.why: Every dose decision depends on who the patient is.

options.t: Indication first, then weight and kidney function later
options.why: Indication is step two; without patient basics (weight, allergy) you cannot judge it.

options.t: Drug first: check the dose against the usual range
options.why: Checking the drug before the patient misses wrong patient, allergy and weight errors.

options.t: Duplicates first: scan the MAR for other anticoagulants
options.why: Duplicate checking is a later step in the routine.

steps.teach: Build the habit: **patient first, then indication, then drug.** Experienced pharmacists check the same things in the same order so nothing gets skipped at 3 a.m.
steps.where: Weight, allergies and age are in the patient banner at the top of the chart in the EHR (St. Mary's uses Cerner, also called Oracle Health). If the weight says "stated" or is missing, ask the nurse for a measured weight.

steps.q: Why does the indication matter for enoxaparin?

options.t: Prophylaxis and treatment doses differ several fold
options.why: 40 mg daily (prophylaxis) vs 1 mg/kg every 12 hours (treatment).

options.t: Indication decides the needle size and injection site
options.why: Administration technique does not depend on indication.

options.t: Indication decides whether anti Xa levels are routine
options.why: Anti Xa levels are for special populations (kidneys, pregnancy, extremes of weight), not set by indication alone.

options.t: Indication only matters for billing and coding
options.why: It drives the dose.

steps.teach: If you cannot name why a drug is ordered, you cannot judge the dose. When the indication is missing, look at the problem list and admission note, then ask.

steps.q: Which lab do you need before you verify enoxaparin?

options.t: Serum creatinine, to estimate CrCl
options.why: Enoxaparin dosing changes below CrCl 30.

options.t: Platelets
options.why: Baseline for HIT and bleeding risk.

options.t: aPTT, to set the enoxaparin dose
options.why: aPTT monitors unfractionated heparin; enoxaparin barely changes it.

options.t: INR, to set the enoxaparin dose
options.why: INR monitors warfarin.

options.t: Hemoglobin A1c
options.why: Not relevant to anticoagulant dosing.

steps.teach: Renal function and platelets are the two labs to check on every anticoagulant. You will learn the Cockcroft Gault formula in the next case.
steps.where: Labs tab in the chart; look at the trend, not just today's number.

steps.q: Her CrCl is 62 mL/min, platelets 210, no clot, no epidural planned, no other anticoagulant. What do you do?

options.t: Verify the order as written
options.why: CrCl 62, normal platelets, no epidural, no duplicates: 40 mg daily is correct.

options.t: Change it to 30 mg daily for her age
options.why: 30 mg daily is the prophylaxis dose when CrCl is below 30, not an age rule.

options.t: Change it to 30 mg every 12 hours
options.why: 30 mg every 12 hours is an orthopedic or trauma prophylaxis regimen.

options.t: Change it to 1 mg/kg every 24 hours
options.why: That is the treatment dose when CrCl is below 30.

steps.teach: Verifying is also a decision. When everything checks out, verify and move on, so you have time for the orders that need you.

cases.monitor: Platelets and hemoglobin periodically, kidney function as it changes, signs of bleeding.
cases.pearl: **Patient, indication, labs, drug, duplicates, then decide.** Same order, every time.

sources.t: FDA label, Lovenox (Sanofi)
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Calculating creatinine clearance
cases.stem: An order needs a renal dose check. Patient: 70 year old man, 80 kg (measured), height 5 ft 10 in, serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL.

steps.q: Which formula do most drug labels use for renal dose adjustments?

options.t: Cockcroft Gault creatinine clearance
options.why: Most labels base renal adjustments on Cockcroft Gault.

options.t: CKD-EPI eGFR (2021, race free)
options.why: eGFR stages kidney disease; many labels and pharmacy protocols still dose by Cockcroft Gault.

options.t: MDRD eGFR
options.why: An older staging equation, not the label dosing standard.

options.t: Schwartz equation
options.why: Used for children.

steps.teach: CrCl (mL/min) = [(140 minus age) x weight in kg] / (72 x SCr), times 0.85 for females.

steps.q: Calculate his CrCl with actual body weight.

options.t: About 49 mL/min
About 44 mL/min
options.why: That uses ideal body weight (73 kg) instead of the actual weight asked for.

options.t: About 41 mL/min
options.why: That applies the 0.85 female factor to a male patient.

options.t: About 78 mL/min
options.why: That uses an SCr of 1.0, a rounding practice sometimes used for low SCr in older adults, not for 1.6.

steps.teach: Write it out every time on paper or in the calculator. Rounding early causes errors.

steps.q: When should you stop and think about which weight to use?

options.t: Obesity, very low weight, or an unlikely weight
options.why: Choose actual, ideal or adjusted weight per protocol.

options.t: Only when the patient is over 65 years old
options.why: Age is already in the formula.

options.t: Only when SCr is above 2.0 mg/dL
options.why: SCr does not decide which weight to use.

options.t: Only for drugs that are dosed in mg/kg
options.why: Weight choice affects CrCl for every renally dosed drug.

steps.teach: Also be careful when creatinine is changing fast (acute kidney injury). A single value can make CrCl look better than it is.
steps.where: St. Mary's renal dosing policy and the pharmacy dosing guide (verify which weight they use).

cases.pearl: **(140 minus age) x kg over 72 x SCr, times 0.85 if female.** Recheck weight choice in obesity.

sources.t: Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Prediction of creatinine clearance from serum creatinine. Nephron 1976;16:31-41
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Missing allergy reaction
cases.stem: A patient has "penicillin" on the allergy list with no reaction listed. Cefazolin is ordered for cellulitis.

steps.q: What is your first move?

options.t: Ask what the reaction actually was
options.why: Most penicillin labels are not true allergy; the reaction decides the next step.

options.t: Change to vancomycin to avoid any cross reactivity
options.why: Vancomycin is less effective for MSSA and strep skin infections.

options.t: Change to clindamycin as the standard alternative
options.why: Clindamycin is for confirmed severe allergy; resistance is common.

options.t: Verify cefazolin; cross reactivity is always zero
options.why: Cefazolin cross reactivity is very low, but you still clarify and document.

steps.teach: "Allergy" lists are often wrong or vague. Clarifying them is one of the highest value things a pharmacist does.
steps.where: Ask the patient or nurse: what happened, how soon after the dose, how was it treated, and have they taken a penicillin or cephalosporin since? Check prior encounters in the chart.

steps.q: The patient says: "I got an itchy rash as a kid. I had cephalexin last year with no problem." What now?

options.t: Verify cefazolin; record the rash and the tolerated cephalexin
options.why: Documentation helps every future prescriber.

options.t: Request vancomycin, since any rash means avoid beta lactams
options.why: A benign childhood rash is low risk.

options.t: Hold the antibiotic until an allergist sees the patient
options.why: Delays treatment for a low risk history.

options.t: Remove the allergy entirely without telling anyone
options.why: Delabeling follows policy and documentation.

steps.teach: Your documentation outlives your shift. Write the reaction, the date and what was tolerated.

cases.pearl: **Every allergy gets a reaction.** No reaction listed means you ask.

sources.t: Brameli, Stone, Phillips. J Allergy Clin Immunol Glob 2024 (cites 2022 drug allergy practice parameter)
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Who do I call?
cases.stem: At 1 a.m. you find a vancomycin order that is double the dose you expect. You need to change it.

steps.q: Who can change the order?

options.t: The prescriber, or the covering prescriber at night
options.why: Only a prescriber (or a protocol) changes an order.

options.t: The charge nurse, after talking with you
options.why: Nurses can relay information but do not change orders.

options.t: You alone, because pharmacists can always change doses
options.why: Only with a pharmacy to dose protocol or collaborative agreement.

options.t: The pharmacy technician entering the order
options.why: Not within technician scope.

steps.teach: At night the daytime prescriber is usually not the one to call. Find out who is covering (night float, hospitalist, on call resident).
steps.where: The chart's care team list, the unit secretary, or the paging directory. Ask the nurse, "Who is covering tonight?"

steps.q: Does St. Mary's let pharmacists adjust vancomycin without calling?

options.t: Check the policy: many hospitals have pharmacy to dose
options.why: If St. Mary's protocol covers vancomycin, you can adjust and document.

options.t: Yes: Florida law lets any pharmacist change any dose
options.why: Changes need a protocol or prescriber authorization.

options.t: No: pharmacists may never change a dose in Florida
options.why: Pharmacy to dose protocols exist.

options.t: Only after the attending signs a new order each day
options.why: Protocols remove that need.

steps.where: Pharmacy policies on the St. Mary's intranet; ask your manager or a senior pharmacist on your first week.

steps.q: The prescriber says, "Just verify it," and you still believe it is unsafe. What next?

options.t: Explain the risk once more with a source, then escalate
options.why: Chain of command when patient safety is at stake.

options.t: Verify it, because the prescriber takes the responsibility
options.why: You share responsibility for what you verify.

options.t: Delete the order and tell the nurse to hold the drug
options.why: Never delete an order unilaterally.

options.t: Verify it but write a note that you disagreed
options.why: Documentation does not protect the patient.

steps.teach: Escalating is not confrontation. Say: "I'm not comfortable verifying this dose because [reason, source]. I'm going to involve my supervisor so we can settle it quickly."
steps.where: Chain of command policy (verify locally). Write down names, times and what was said.

cases.call: **S:** This is [name], the pharmacist, calling about [patient] in [room]. **B:** Vancomycin 2,500 mg every 12 hours is ordered; weight 70 kg, creatinine 1.4. **A:** That is about double the usual dose for this weight and kidney function, which raises the risk of kidney injury. **R:** I recommend [dose] and a level [when]. Can I change it?
cases.pearl: **Prescriber changes orders. Nurse gives information. Supervisor helps when you disagree.**

sources.t: IHI: SBAR toolkit
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: The MAR
cases.stem: A nurse calls: "Did the patient get the 0600 antibiotic? The day nurse isn't sure."

steps.q: Where do you look?

options.t: The MAR (medication administration record)
options.why: Shows what was given and when.

options.t: The active order in the order profile
options.why: Shows what should be given, not what was.

options.t: The dispensing cabinet removal log
options.why: Shows what was removed, not given.

options.t: The pharmacy verification history
options.why: Shows what you verified.

steps.teach: Learn the difference: **ordered** (order), **dispensed** (pharmacy or cabinet), **given** (MAR). Errors live in the gaps between them.
steps.where: MAR tab in the chart. Look for "given," "not given," "held" and the reason.

steps.q: The MAR shows the dose as "not given, patient off unit." What matters most now?

options.t: Give the dose as soon as possible and retime the next dose
options.why: For time sensitive antibiotics, the missed dose matters most.

options.t: File an event report first, then give the dose
options.why: Report after the patient is safe.

options.t: Skip the dose and give the next one on schedule
options.why: A missed antibiotic dose can fail treatment.

options.t: Give a double dose at the next scheduled time
options.why: Never double to catch up.

sources.t: St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: The automated dispensing cabinet override
cases.stem: An ED nurse removed a drug from the automated dispensing cabinet (often called Pyxis or Omnicell) on override before you verified the order.

steps.q: When is a cabinet override appropriate?

options.t: True emergencies using drugs on the approved override list
options.why: Joint Commission expects policies and override review.

options.t: Any time the pharmacist has not verified within 15 minutes
options.why: Delay alone is not an emergency.

options.t: Any drug, as long as a second nurse witnesses it
options.why: Witnessing is for controlled substance waste, not override rules.

options.t: Never; every dose must be verified first
options.why: Overrides exist for emergencies.

steps.teach: The Joint Commission expects hospitals to have policies for dispensing cabinets and to review overrides.
steps.where: St. Mary's automated dispensing cabinet policy and override list (verify locally).

steps.q: What is your job after an override?

options.t: Review the order as if not yet given, and follow up
options.why: Your review still matters for the next doses.

options.t: Nothing, because the dose was already given
options.why: Future doses and errors still need review.

options.t: Report the nurse for using override
options.why: Overrides in emergencies are appropriate.

options.t: Reverse the dispense in the cabinet
options.why: Inventory fixes do not replace clinical review.

cases.pearl: **Override is for emergencies. You still review it.**

sources.t: Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (LAMMICO summary)
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Five pages at once
cases.stem: At 2 a.m. these all arrive in the same 5 minutes: (1) a code blue page, (2) a nurse asking if a tablet can be crushed, (3) a STAT tenecteplase request for a stroke alert, (4) a routine antibiotic order, (5) a question about a drug interaction for a discharge tomorrow.

steps.q: Which do you handle first?

options.t: The code and the stroke alert together (call backup)
options.why: Both are life threatening and time critical.

options.t: The STAT antibiotic, since first doses are time sensitive
options.why: Important, but after life threatening events.

options.t: The crush question, since it takes 30 seconds
options.why: Fast does not beat life threatening.

options.t: The queue in order received, to be fair to everyone
options.why: Triage by harm if delayed.

steps.teach: Sort by **harm if delayed**: life threatening now, then time sensitive (first antibiotic doses, STAT orders), then routine, then questions for later.
steps.where: St. Mary's code and stroke alert response policies tell you which pharmacist responds (verify locally).

steps.q: After the emergencies, what is next?

options.t: The new antibiotic order (time sensitive first dose)
The discharge interaction question for tomorrow
options.why: Can wait.

options.t: The crush question before the antibiotic
options.why: The first dose is more time sensitive.

options.t: Documentation of the code before anything else
options.why: Document after time sensitive care.

steps.q: The crush question: how do you answer it fast and correctly?

options.t: ISMP Do Not Crush list and the exact product
options.why: Extended release and enteric coated products are classic no crush.

options.t: Trissel's IV compatibility for the tablet
options.why: Trissel's covers IV compatibility, not crushing.

options.t: LactMed entry for the drug being crushed
options.why: Breastfeeding reference.

options.t: The pregnancy and lactation label section
options.why: Unrelated to crushing.

steps.where: ISMP Do Not Crush list, the drug label, or Lexicomp through St. Mary's.

cases.pearl: **Life threatening, then time sensitive, then routine, then questions.**

sources.t: ISMP: High alert medications in acute care settings
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Answering a drug information question
cases.stem: A nurse asks: "Can I give this IV drug through the same line as the heparin drip?"

steps.q: What do you ask before you answer?

options.t: Which drug, its concentration, and what else runs
options.why: Compatibility depends on all three.

options.t: How long the heparin drip has been running
options.why: Not the compatibility question.

options.t: The patient's weight and kidney function
options.why: Dosing, not compatibility.

options.t: Whether the line is peripheral or central
options.why: Line type matters for some drugs, but you need the drugs and concentrations.

steps.teach: Systematic approach: get the background, figure out the real question, search, answer clearly, and document.

steps.q: Where do you look for Y site compatibility?

options.t: Trissel's or the King Guide (or free Stabilis)
LactMed (NIH) drug compatibility pages
options.why: LactMed covers breastfeeding only.

options.t: The ISMP Do Not Crush list for IV drugs
options.why: Oral dosage forms only.

options.t: NeoFax neonatal dosing monographs only
options.why: Dosing reference; some compatibility, not the primary source.

steps.where: See your IV Compatibility page in the Drug Hub for the classic ones.

steps.q: You cannot find data for this pair. What do you tell the nurse?

options.t: No data: do not run them together; separate line or flush
options.why: Absence of data is treated as incompatible.

options.t: No data: probably fine if the concentrations are low
options.why: Concentration can change compatibility, but no data means avoid.

options.t: No data: run them together and watch for cloudiness
options.why: Precipitates can be invisible.

options.t: No data: mix them in the same bag instead
options.why: Admixture compatibility is a separate, stricter question.

sources.t: ASHP guidelines on the pharmacist's role in providing drug information

cases.title: High alert drug double check
cases.stem: An insulin infusion is ordered. It is on the ISMP high alert list.

steps.q: What does "high alert" mean?

options.t: Errors with these drugs are more likely to cause harm
options.why: ISMP definition.

options.t: They are the most often prescribed drugs
options.why: Frequency is not the definition.

options.t: They need a second pharmacist to verify by law
options.why: Double checks are policy based, not a legal definition.

options.t: They are all controlled substances
options.why: Many are not (insulin, heparin).

steps.q: Which safeguards help most with high alert infusions?

options.t: Standard concentrations matched to the pump library
Independent double checks where policy requires them
Premixed bags when available
Custom concentrations for each patient's fluid needs
options.why: Custom concentrations defeat pump safety limits.

options.t: Storing insulin vials next to heparin vials for speed
options.why: Look alike storage causes mix ups.

cases.pearl: **High alert = high harm when wrong.** Standardize, use the pump library, double check.

sources.t: ISMP: High alert medications in acute care settings

cases.title: Do Not Use abbreviations
cases.stem: An order reads: "Insulin regular 10U IV x1" and another reads "Morphine 2.0 mg IV q4h PRN."

steps.q: What is wrong with these orders?

options.t: "U" can be misread as 0 or 4: write "units"
A trailing zero (2.0 mg) can be misread as 20 mg
"IV" must be written as "intravenous"
options.why: "IV" is acceptable; "IU" is the Do Not Use item.

options.t: "PRN" is on the Do Not Use list
options.why: PRN is acceptable.

steps.q: What should you write for a dose under 1 mg?

options.t: A leading zero: 0.5 mg
No zero: .5 mg
options.why: The decimal can be missed: read as 5 mg.

options.t: A trailing zero: 0.50 mg
options.why: Trailing zeros are on the Do Not Use list.

options.t: A fraction: 1/2 mg
options.why: Fractions invite misreading.

cases.pearl: **No U, no IU, no trailing zero, always a leading zero.**

sources.t: Joint Commission Do Not Use list (Becker's summary)

cases.title: Reporting a near miss
cases.stem: You caught a 10 fold heparin error before it reached the patient.

steps.q: Should you report it?

options.t: Yes: report near misses in St. Mary's reporting system
options.why: Near misses show system weaknesses for free.

options.t: No: reports are only for errors that reached the patient
options.why: Near misses are reported too.

options.t: Only if the prescriber agrees to the report
options.why: No permission needed.

options.t: Only to ISMP, not internally
options.why: Internal reporting comes first; ISMP reporting is optional and voluntary.

steps.teach: In a just culture, human error gets support, at risk behavior gets coaching, and reckless behavior gets action. Reports fix systems, not people.
steps.where: St. Mary's event reporting system (verify the name and how to access it). ISMP also accepts voluntary reports.

cases.pearl: **Report near misses. They are free lessons.**

sources.t: ISMP
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Shift handoff
cases.stem: You are leaving at 7 a.m. You are waiting on a vancomycin level, and a prescriber promised to call back about a duplicate order.

steps.q: What goes in your handoff?

options.t: Pending items, who you wait on, and what to do if no callback
options.why: Hand off what is pending, not what is done.

options.t: Only what you finished, so nothing gets repeated
options.why: Finished work needs no handoff.

options.t: Nothing; the next pharmacist will find it in the queue
options.why: Callbacks are not in the queue.

options.t: Everything you did on the shift in time order
options.why: Too long; the next pharmacist needs the open items.

cases.pearl: **Hand off what is pending, not what is done.**

sources.t: IHI: SBAR toolkit

cases.title: Home medication reconciliation
cases.stem: A new admission lists "metoprolol, a water pill, and something for sugar." The team wants an accurate home list.

steps.q: Which sources make the home list accurate?

options.t: The patient or family, using open questions
Outpatient pharmacy fill history or a call to the pharmacy
Pill bottles brought from home
The last discharge summary from 2 years ago, as is
options.why: Useful as a starting point, but out of date without confirmation.

options.t: The usual dose for each drug class
options.why: Guessing creates errors.

steps.q: Why does it matter in the hospital?

options.t: Missed home drugs cause withdrawal; errors carry to discharge
options.why: For example beta blocker withdrawal.

options.t: It only matters for billing and insurance
It only matters for controlled substances
It only matters after discharge, not during the stay
options.why: Inpatient omissions cause harm too.

cases.pearl: **Ask the person, check the pharmacy, see the bottles.**

sources.t: Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (LAMMICO summary)

cases.title: A drug is on shortage
cases.stem: The supplier says a drug you use often is on shortage.

steps.q: Where do you look for alternatives and the plan?

options.t: ASHP shortage list plus St. Mary's substitution protocol
options.why: Joint Commission expects written substitution protocols.

options.t: FDA Orange Book therapeutic equivalence ratings
options.why: The Orange Book lists generic equivalence, not shortage alternatives.

options.t: The FDA Purple Book
options.why: Biologic and biosimilar listings.

options.t: Each prescriber chooses their own substitute
options.why: Uncoordinated substitution causes errors.

steps.where: ASHP Drug Shortages (ashp.org/drug-shortages), St. Mary's pharmacy leadership and P&T announcements.

cases.pearl: **Shortage = status check, approved substitute, clear communication.**

sources.t: ASHP Drug Shortages
Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (LAMMICO summary)
